raw_response:
Switching can make sense if GitHub outages repeatedly prevent your actual work, but the evidence gathered here does not establish that another provider has better uptime. With collaboration style, CI requirements, budget, and willingness to operate servers unspecified, I would first test one representative repository and an independent copy of its Git history. A complete move becomes attractive when the replacement handles your review and release workflow and the expected reduction in disruption outweighs migration and maintenance work.

My ranked shortlist is below. The ranking reflects general usefulness for this question, not measured reliability.

1. GitLab — the first managed alternative I would evaluate for an existing GitHub collaboration workflow.
https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/import/github/

GitLab's GitHub importer can transfer repository data and substantial collaboration metadata, including issues, pull requests, comments, labels, milestones, and wiki pages. It supports GitLab.com and self-managed offerings. This gives you a practical migration path when preserving existing project discussion matters. Its documentation identifies import limitations and does not migrate GitHub organizations or groups. Test attribution, links, attachments, permissions, and CI separately on a representative project before committing to a move. An importer is evidence of migration capability, not evidence of superior availability.

2. Codeberg — a hosted option to investigate for a free-software project.
https://docs.codeberg.org/getting-started/what-is-codeberg/

Codeberg is a nonprofit, community-run forge based on Forgejo. Its migration tool supports GitHub repository data and metadata such as issues, labels, wiki content, releases, and milestones:
https://docs.codeberg.org/advanced/migrating-repos/

The decisive caveat is CI. Codeberg's current documentation describes manually approved Woodpecker access, limited shared resources, an as-is availability caveat, and limited hosted Forgejo Actions availability:
https://docs.codeberg.org/ci/

That makes Codeberg worth testing for an eligible project, but CI continuity cannot be inferred from the presence of a hosting service. Check whether its project scope and available runners fit your workload; use your own runner only if you are willing to operate it.

3. Forgejo — an option when control of the hosting environment is a central requirement.
https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/admin/installation/

Forgejo is self-hostable forge software; its installation documentation covers binaries and Docker. This lets you choose infrastructure and operational policies instead of depending entirely on another public hosting provider. The tradeoff is responsibility for service operation, updates, backups, recovery, and runners. Self-hosting only improves your situation if you can operate the required service adequately. Forgejo Actions provides CI, but its documentation explicitly distinguishes familiarity from GitHub Actions compatibility, so existing workflows need validation:
https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/user/actions/overview/

4. SourceHut — an alternative for people comfortable with email-oriented contribution and review.
https://sourcehut.org/

SourceHut offers Git hosting, ticket tracking, mailing-list-based patch review, and virtualized CI builds. Its workflow is materially different from a GitHub pull-request-centered setup, so contributor acceptance is an important part of a trial. Its current site describes the service as a public alpha. Its pricing page expects project hosts to pay according to means, offers financial assistance, and identifies builds as a paid service during the alpha:
https://sourcehut.org/pricing/

I would evaluate SourceHut if that collaboration model is appealing, rather than assume a repository import preserves the existing contributor experience.

5. Gitea repository mirroring — a useful mechanism if the immediate objective is reducing dependence on a single code host.
https://docs.gitea.com/usage/repository/repo-mirror/

Gitea supports periodic pull and push mirrors of commits, branches, and tags. An independently hosted pull mirror can provide an additional copy while you evaluate a full switch; after moving, a push mirror can retain a GitHub copy. The public implementation shows scheduled synchronization and error handling:
https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/main/services/mirror/mirror_pull.go

Keep one authoritative write location. Mirroring is not automatic failover for issues, reviews, CI, or releases, and a pull mirror cannot acquire new changes while its source is unavailable. The documentation also warns that push mirroring overwrites remote changes.

A concrete trial should exercise clone and push, one review, an issue with attachments, the normal build, and the normal release. Compare the migration effort and ongoing operating burden with the disruption you actually experience. If outages mainly interrupt Git access, a separate copy may provide enough value with a smaller transition. If the blocked work is reviews or release automation, test those services explicitly before switching.

Evidence limits: this is a capability and migration shortlist, not an uptime study or a demonstration that any option was deployed successfully. The sources are live pages retrieved after the question's 2026-08-17 cutoff; their historical feature availability was not independently established, so date status is unknown. One unauthenticated grep.app search attempt was inaccessible. Gitea source was instead located using public code indexed in web search; that is code-through-web fallback, not successful native code search.
